title: Popular Resistance to the British Rule
summary: ## Causes and nature of early resistance (1750–1857)

People resist when their rights are taken away. British policies hurt displaced rulers, zamindars, poligars, peasants and tribals: heavy land revenue, loss of land to moneylenders, forced commercial crops and interference in religion. Examples: the people of Banaras rose when Warren Hastings imprisoned Raja Chet Singh; the Poligars of Madras rebelled when their military and land rights were taken. The movements used violence and plunder against exploiters and mainly aimed to restore the old structures and relations. From 1763 to 1856 there were more than 40 major rebellions, but they were local and isolated from each other.

Faqir and Sanyasi Rebellions (1770–1820s, Bengal): after the Bengal famine of 1770, landless peasants, displaced zamindars and disbanded soldiers joined the Sanyasis and Faqirs (wandering Muslim mendicants). Leaders included Majnum Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani; they attacked English factories. The immediate cause of the Sanyasi revolt was British restrictions on pilgrims.

Indigo Rebellion (1859–62, Bengal): indigo farmers were discontented because they got very low prices, indigo was sown at the same time as food crops, and it reduced soil fertility. Hindu and Muslim peasants refused to grow indigo and filed cases, supported by the press and missionaries; in November 1860 the government declared forced indigo cultivation illegal.

Farazi Movement (1838–48): the first no-tax campaign, led by Shariatullah Khan and Dadu Mian against planters and zamindars. Wahabi Movement (1830s–60s): led by Syed Ahmed Barelvi of Rae Bareli, influenced by Abdul Wahab and Shah Waliullah; religious in origin, it became a class struggle of peasants against landlords. Peasant revolts did not aim to end British rule, but they created awareness and prepared the ground for 1857.

British policies destroyed the self-sufficient tribal economy based on land and forests. Santhal Rebellion (1855–57, Santhal Pargana/Daman-i-Koh): moneylenders and traders made Santhals bonded labourers; Sidhu and Kanu led a heroic revolt that was crushed. Munda Rebellion (1899–1900, Chhotanagpur): led by Birsa Munda against contractors, moneylenders and missionaries; he died in prison in 1900, but the Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) gave land rights and banned bonded labour. Jaintia and Garo Rebellion (1860s–70s, Meghalaya): they opposed a strategic road from the Brahmaputra valley to Sylhet and new house and income taxes; Jaintia leader U Kiang Nongbah was hanged and Garo leader Pa Togan Sangma defeated. Bhil uprising (1818–31, Khandesh), Kol uprising (1831–32, Singhbhum) and Mappila uprisings (1836–54, Malabar) against British land laws and landlords.

Political causes: annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Nagpur, Jhansi) and Subsidiary Alliance; Nana Saheb was denied Baji Rao II's pension; Awadh was annexed on grounds of misgovernment, leaving many jobless. Economic causes: ruin of handicrafts, drain of wealth, heavy land revenue, loss of land to moneylenders and frequent famines. Social and religious causes: social reforms and missionary activity were seen as attempts to convert people; Act XXI of 1850 let converts inherit property. Military causes: Indian soldiers could not rise above the rank of subedar, were paid less than the English, were denied overseas allowance (bhatta) and feared losing caste by crossing the 'black water'.

Immediate cause: the Enfield rifle's greased cartridges, rumoured to contain cow and pig fat, which had to be bitten. Mangal Pandey was the first sepoy to openly disobey orders, killing two officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857. On 10 May 1857 sepoys at Meerut revolted, marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar Emperor of India. Leaders: Nana Saheb (Kanpur, with Tantya Tope and Azimullah), Begum Hazrat Mahal and Maulvi Ahmadullah (Lucknow), Rani Lakshmi Bai (Jhansi), Kunwar Singh (Arrah), Khan Bahadur Khan (Bareilly). The British retook Delhi in September 1857 and Lord Canning proclaimed the end of the revolt on 8 July 1858. Bahadur Shah was exiled to Rangoon.

Nature: begun by sepoys but joined by peasants and artisans; marked by Hindu–Muslim unity — the first national struggle for independence. Causes of failure: no unity of purpose (each leader fought for his own territory), confined to North and Central India (Punjab, Rajputana, Madras and Bombay stayed away; many rulers helped the British), weak leadership and planning, shortage of weapons and money, and British control of the telegraph and the sea.

By the Act for the Better Government of India (August 1858) Company rule ended and the Crown took over; a Secretary of State with a 15-member council was created and the Governor-General became the Viceroy. Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858) promised to honour treaties and allowed adoption. The army was reorganised with more European troops and native was played against native; the British adopted a policy of Divide and Rule. The Indian Civil Service Act (1861) and the Indian Councils Act (1861) followed. The revolt sowed the seeds of nationalism and gave India heroes, though racial bitterness was its worst legacy.

vsa: Explain any two reasons for the growing discontent among farmers growing indigo during British rule.
(1) They were paid very low prices for indigo by the planters. (2) Indigo had to be sown at the same time as food crops and it reduced the fertility of the soil, so food production fell.

or: Name the leader of the Wahabi movement and explain the significance of the movement.

It was led by Syed Ahmed Barelvi of Rae Bareli. Though religious in origin, it became a class struggle in which peasants, irrespective of religion, united against their landlords, adding to anti-British feeling.

vsa: Describe the Jaintia and Garo Rebellion in brief.

After the First Anglo-Burmese War the British planned a strategic road from the Brahmaputra valley to Sylhet. The Jaintias and Garos of present Meghalaya opposed it from 1827; the British burnt their villages and the anger grew with new house and income taxes in the 1860s. Jaintia leader U Kiang Nongbah was hanged and Garo leader Pa Togan Sangma defeated.
Explain one social and one religious cause of the Revolt of 1857.

Social: reforms such as the ban on sati, widow remarriage and women's education were seen as interference in Indian customs, and Indians were treated with contempt. Religious: missionary schools and Act XXI of 1850 (which let converts inherit property) made people fear forced conversion; sepoys feared losing caste by crossing the sea.
List two grievances of the Indian sepoys against the British.

(1) They were paid less than English soldiers, could not rise above subedar and were often denied bhatta for overseas service. (2) Their religious feelings were hurt — they were ordered to remove caste marks, serve overseas, and finally to use greased cartridges.
Why is the Revolt of 1857 called the first national struggle for independence?

(1) Though begun by the sepoys, it was joined by peasants, artisans and others, and people of many regions fought together against the British. (2) It was marked by Hindu–Muslim unity — the rebels even proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as Emperor of India. It sowed the seeds of nationalism and gave India heroes.
sa: Explain the causes of the early resistance movements against British rule in India before the Revolt of 1857.

(1) British policies took away the rights, status and land of displaced rulers, zamindars and poligars. (2) Heavy land revenue, eviction and exploitation by moneylenders and forced commercial crops ruined peasants. (3) Tribals lost their land and forests to traders and moneylenders. (4) Interference in religious practices angered people. They aimed to restore old structures and resist outside interference.

or: Explain the causes of the revolt of the Poligars of Madras.

The Poligars were local chiefs in the Madras Presidency who held military and land rights. When the British tried to take away these rights, disband their armed retainers and collect revenue directly, they lost their power and income, so they rebelled; the British crushed them.

sa: Describe the Faqir and Sanyasi Rebellions of 1770–1820s.

After British control of Bengal, land revenue rose and the Bengal famine of 1770 caused misery. Peasants whose land was confiscated, displaced zamindars and disbanded soldiers joined the Sanyasis and Faqirs (wandering Muslim mendicants). Leaders like Majnum Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani attacked English factories and seized goods and arms; restrictions on pilgrims were the immediate cause. The British crushed them by the early 19th century.
Explain four reasons why the peasants revolted against British rule.

(1) High land revenue under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements. (2) Loss of land to moneylenders (mahajans) charging high interest, making peasants bonded labourers. (3) Forced cultivation of commercial crops like indigo at low prices, reducing food and causing famines. (4) Harassment by officials, zamindars and middlemen and no access to justice.
Why did the Revolt of 1857 fail? Explain.

(1) No unity of purpose: leaders fought for their own territories — the Mughal throne, the Peshwaship, Jhansi. (2) It was confined to North and Central India; Punjab, Rajputana, Madras and Bombay stayed away and many rulers and the educated classes helped the British. (3) Weak leadership, poor planning and lack of coordination. (4) Shortage of modern weapons and money, while the British had the telegraph and control of the sea.
Explain the impact of the Revolt of 1857 on India.

(1) East India Company rule ended and the Crown took direct control (1858). (2) The army was reorganised with more Europeans and fewer Indians; Indian artillery was disbanded. (3) The British followed 'Divide and Rule' between Hindus and Muslims. (4) Indian rulers were assured of their states and right of adoption. (5) It sowed the seeds of nationalism and gave India national heroes.
Describe the Munda Rebellion and its significance.

The Mundas, the original clearers of the forest, enjoyed special land rights, which were destroyed by merchants, moneylenders and British contractors who made them indentured labourers. Birsa Munda, who had some missionary education, led them (1899–1900), attacked police stations and churches, and urged them to protect their sacred groves. He died in prison in 1900, but the Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) gave tribals land rights and banned bonded labour.
la: Describe the political, economic, social and military causes of the Revolt of 1857.

Political: (1) Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance annexed states like Satara, Nagpur and Jhansi; Nana Saheb was denied his pension and Awadh was annexed, leaving soldiers and officials jobless. Economic: (2) Handicrafts were ruined and wealth drained; (3) heavy land revenue made peasants lose land to moneylenders, and famines followed. Social-religious: (4) reforms and missionary activity and Act XXI of 1850 made people fear conversion. Military: (5) sepoys were paid less, denied promotion and bhatta, and forced to serve overseas. Immediate: (6) greased cartridges believed to contain cow and pig fat hurt both Hindus and Muslims.
Explain the nature and significance of the Revolt of 1857.

(1) It began as a revolt of sepoys but was joined by peasants, artisans and rulers, so it became a popular revolt. (2) Hindus and Muslims, landlords and peasants fought together against a common enemy. (3) Rebels of different regions helped each other; it is called the First War of Independence. (4) It ended the East India Company's rule and the Crown took over in 1858. (5) The British changed their army and policies, adopting Divide and Rule. (6) Though it failed, it sowed the seeds of nationalism and inspired later struggles.
